My best prediction is that it would **change Ryan’s code from SC to UA**, record his explanation in a note, and probably email HR or his team leader to flag the consequences.

A typical rule-following assistant would read the categories literally: Ryan expressly says he was not ill; his sister does not fall within the stated DEP definition because she is neither one of the listed relatives nor someone in his household; and none of the other codes fits. Calling before his shift satisfies the notification expectation, but does not itself make the absence authorised.

**That would trigger the termination letter at noon**, because this is his second UA during probation. Adding a sympathetic note or sending an escalation email would not stop that outcome unless someone actually intervened before payroll.

That is a prediction of likely procedural behaviour—not a claim that dismissal would be fair or legally justified.
